data.title: Christian and Islamic Festivals
data.sourcePassage: The Christian calendar is shaped around the life of Jesus. Advent is the four-week season of preparation and expectation before Christmas (25 December), when Christians celebrate the incarnation — the belief that God became human in Jesus. Advent is not a fast but a time of waiting and hope. Christmas focuses not on presents but on the theological event of God entering human history. Easter is the most important festival in the Christian year, far surpassing Christmas in theological significance. It follows Holy Week, which includes Palm Sunday, Maundy Thursday (the Last Supper), and Good Friday (the crucifixion). Easter Sunday celebrates the resurrection — Jesus rising from the dead — which Christians believe is the foundation of all Christian hope. Before Easter, Christians observe Lent: a 40-day period of fasting, prayer, and self-examination, recalling Jesus's 40 days in the wilderness. Islam does not have the same calendar cycle but observes two major festivals. Ramadan is not a festival but a month — the ninth month of the Islamic lunar calendar — dedicated to fasting (sawm) from dawn to sunset, increased prayer, and recitation of the Qur'an. It commemorates the month in which the Qur'an was first revealed to the Prophet Muhammad. At the end of Ramadan comes Eid al-Fitr ('Festival of Breaking the Fast'), celebrated with communal prayers, feasting, charity (Zakat al-Fitr), and family gatherings. Eid al-Adha ('Festival of Sacrifice') occurs approximately two months later, during the season of Hajj. It remembers Ibrahim's (Abraham's) willingness to sacrifice his son in obedience to God — and God's provision of a ram in his place. Muslims celebrate with prayers and the sharing of meat with family, neighbours, and those in need.

data.title: Jewish and Hindu Festivals
data.sourcePassage: The Jewish festival calendar is rich and theologically significant. The year begins with Rosh Hashanah (Jewish New Year) — two days of prayer, reflection, and the sounding of the shofar (ram's horn), calling Jews to self-examination. It begins ten days of repentance that culminate in Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement — the holiest day of the year. Yom Kippur involves a 25-hour fast, five prayer services, and the seeking of forgiveness from God and from those one has wronged. Jewish tradition holds that on this day God seals the fate of each person for the coming year. Pesach (Passover) is perhaps the most widely observed Jewish festival, commemorating the Exodus from Egypt — when God freed the Israelites from slavery under Pharaoh. Families gather for the Seder, a ritual meal at which the Exodus story is retold using the Haggadah (a special text), symbolic foods (bitter herbs for slavery, matzah for haste), and the Four Questions asked by the youngest child. Hanukkah is a minor festival — but it is often wrongly presented as the Jewish equivalent of Christmas simply because it occurs in December. It commemorates the rededication of the Temple in Jerusalem. Its eight days of candle-lighting are meaningful but do not carry the same weight as Yom Kippur or Pesach. Hindu festivals are joyful occasions that mark key mythological events. Diwali — the Festival of Lights — celebrates the return of Rama and Sita after defeating the demon king Ravana, and the welcome of Lakshmi, goddess of prosperity. Homes are lit with diyas (small clay lamps) and fireworks are set off to represent the victory of light over darkness and good over evil. Holi is the Festival of Colours, celebrated at the start of spring and associated with the story of Prahlad's devotion to Vishnu and his miraculous survival of an attempt by his demon aunt Holika to burn him alive.

data.title: Sikh and Buddhist Festivals
data.sourcePassage: Vaisakhi is the most important festival in the Sikh calendar, celebrated on 13 or 14 April. It marks the founding of the Khalsa — the community of initiated, committed Sikhs — by Guru Gobind Singh at Anandpur in 1699. On that day, the Guru called for volunteers willing to give their lives for their faith; five men came forward and became the Panj Pyare (Beloved Five), the first members of the Khalsa. Vaisakhi is celebrated with Nagar Kirtan (street processions of the Guru Granth Sahib), Akhand Path (continuous reading of the Guru Granth Sahib over 48 hours), kirtan in the gurdwara, and langar for all. Gurpurbs are Sikh holy days marking the births or martyrdoms of the ten Gurus. Guru Nanak's Gurpurb, celebrating the founder of Sikhism, is widely observed. Bandi Chhor Divas ('Day of Liberation') marks the release of Guru Hargobind from Mughal imprisonment and coincides with the Hindu festival of Diwali — both traditions celebrate with lights. Vesak (also called Wesak or Buddha Day) is the most important festival in the Buddhist calendar. It is observed on the full moon of May and commemorates three key events in the Buddha's life: his birth as Prince Siddhattha Gotama, his enlightenment (Bodhi) under the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya, and his final passing away (parinirvana). In Theravada Buddhism, all three events are held to have occurred on the same date in different years. Vesak is observed with lantern processions, temple visits, meditation, offerings, and acts of generosity. Focusing on the Buddha's life during Vesak encourages reflection on the qualities he embodied — wisdom, compassion, and liberation — that Buddhists aspire to develop.
